comparedAgainst: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, the DNS section of the application-layer chapter
justification: No verified factual error, so not capped at 7; held below 8.5 by a cluster of real, checkable issues rather than by any wrong claim. Source verification: I fetched the raw text of RFC 1034, RFC 1035, RFC 8499, RFC 2308, RFC 2606, RFC 5737 and RFC 3596 myself and checked every quoted or paraphrased sentence against them by section number. Every quote matched verbatim, including two RFC 1035 quirks the article reproduces faithfully (the 'this be is set' typo in the RA bit definition, and the elided '...' in the CNAME/NS RDATA quotes). Section numbers cited (1034 3.6, 4.2, 4.3.1; 1035 3.2.2, 4.1.1, 4.2.1; 8499 section 6 and 7; 2308 section 3 and 5; 2606 section 2) all check out against the RFCs' actual section headers. The Microsoft Learn quotes (GetHostAddresses IPv6 filtering remark, GetHostEntry's HostNotFound/11001 remark distinguishing 'DNS server does not respond' from 'cannot be found in the database') are both verbatim on the live pages. The IANA root-servers claim (13 letter-named services, anycast, hundreds of physical machines) is supported by the live page. Code verification: run-code passed 5/5 consecutive runs with identical block counts, so the wildcarding of network-dependent output is doing its job (no flakiness across 5 runs on this network). I also extracted the walk program and the failure-modes program and ran them independently outside the harness: the walk reproduced the article's exact claimed path (root -> 6 NS referral to .org -> 4 NS referral to iana.org's servers -> CNAME to www.iana.org.cdn.cloudflare.net) and glue IP 199.4.138.53, which I confirmed via nslookup really is ns.icann.org, one of iana.org's real authoritative servers; the failure-modes program reproduced NXDOMAIN (rcode=3), a genuine 3-second timeout against 192.0.2.1 (TEST-NET-1), and a SERVFAIL (rcode=2) from the loopback fake server, matching the article's claimed output exactly. I independently queried iana.org's authoritative server for MX and NS records and got the same four pechora*.icann.org MX hosts and four NS hosts the article shows, with the same TTLs (86400 for NS, 3600 for MX). The wire-format parsing (header layout, AA/RA bit positions, RDATA offsets for A/NS/CNAME/MX, name-compression pointer handling) is correct RFC 1035 section 4.1 byte-for-byte; I checked it by hand. The article's structure matches CONTENT_PLAN.md row 4 (shape Q: hierarchy -> recursive vs iterative -> record types -> TTL/caching -> failure modes) exactly. What keeps it out of 8.5+ territory: an unsourced 'most common mistake' superlative that the editorial brief's binding pilot lessons explicitly forbid, an unscoped 'all leave RA clear' generalization about authoritative servers as a class (true for the root/TLD examples shown, not true as an absolute), and a two-way sourcing-hygiene gap (RFC 5737 sits in front matter but is never cited inline in prose; RFC 3596 is cited inline for AAAA=28 but is missing from front matter) that the brief's pilot lessons call out by name as a finding in its own right.

issues.location: Opening paragraph, sentence 2 ('mixing up which side does which is the single most common way people get DNS wrong')
issues.problem: Unsourced claim about the relative frequency of a misconception. The editorial brief's binding pilot lessons are explicit: 'No "what most people think" claims unless sourced. No asserted experience ("this fails in production", "the two are confused constantly").' None of the nine sources in front matter supports a claim about what is 'the single most common' DNS mistake; it reads as an assertion of the writer's own experience.
issues.fixLooksLike: Drop the superlative. State the distinction and let the failure-modes section's own evidence carry the weight, e.g. 'Those are two different resolution styles, layered, and the rest of this article depends on keeping them straight' — no claim about prevalence, sourced or otherwise.

issues.location: 'What's the difference between a recursive resolver and an iterative one?', final sentence ('root, TLD and authoritative servers all leave RA clear')
issues.problem: Unscoped absolute claim about 'authoritative servers' as a category. RA is a per-server configuration choice, not something the protocol ties to a server's role (RFC 1034 section 4.3.1: 'The bit is true if the name server is willing to provide recursive service for the client'). Root and TLD operators leave RA clear as settled policy (confirmed empirically: my own query to 198.41.0.4 returned ra=false), but nothing prevents, and real deployments sometimes run, an authoritative server that also offers recursion (the 'open resolver' anti-pattern). The claim as written generalizes from two verified cases to a whole category.
issues.fixLooksLike: Scope it to what is actually demonstrated: 'root and TLD servers, by policy, leave RA clear, and so does any authoritative server run according to current best practice' — or drop 'authoritative servers' from the absolute list and treat it as the operational norm rather than a guarantee.

issues.location: Front matter 'sources' vs. inline citations for RFC 5737 (TEST-NET-1) and RFC 3596 (AAAA type)
issues.problem: Two-way sourcing gap that the brief's binding pilot lessons name directly: 'A source in the list that is never cited inline ... is a finding.' RFC 5737 is listed in front matter and used to justify 192.0.2.1 as a documentation address, but it is never cited inline in prose with a link — it appears only in a C# code comment ('192.0.2.1 is TEST-NET-1') and in an uncited prose sentence ('as the TEST-NET-1 case simulates'). Conversely, the record-type table cites 'RFC 3596, not RFC 1035' for AAAA=28 inline, but RFC 3596 is absent from the sources list entirely, so there is no front-matter record that it was actually fetched and read (I fetched it myself and confirmed AAAA=28 is defined in its section 2.1, so the underlying fact is correct — this is a process gap, not a wrong claim).
issues.fixLooksLike: Add one inline citation with a link near the TEST-NET-1 mentions (e.g., in the failure-modes decision-procedure bullet: '([RFC 5737, section 3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5737.html#section-3))'), and add RFC 3596 to the front-matter sources list with an accessed date, since the article already relies on and cites it.

issues.location: 'What's the difference between a recursive resolver and an iterative one?', first paragraph, the quote 'the first server pursues the query for the client at another server' attributed to RFC 8499 section 6
issues.problem: The quote is verbatim and does live in RFC 8499 section 6 (confirmed by direct text search), so the citation is not wrong, but it is RFC 8499's definition of 'Recursive mode' (itself quoting RFC 1034 section 2.3), not its definition of 'recursive query'. RFC 8499's actual 'Recursive query' entry in the same section reads: 'A query with the Recursion Desired (RD) bit set to 1 in the header. ... If recursive service is available and is requested by the RD bit in the query, the server uses its resolver to answer the query.' The article uses the mode quote to characterize the query itself.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either attribute the quote explicitly to recursive mode ('RFC 8499 describes a server operating in recursive mode this way: ...') or pair it with the adjacent RD-bit definition so the reader sees both what makes a query recursive (the RD bit) and what the server that receives one then does.

issues.location: Program id=walk, the line `server = s.glueIp;` inside the hop loop
issues.problem: If a referral's additional section carries no A record for any delegated server (glueIp stays ""), the next loop iteration calls `IPAddress.Parse("")`, which throws an unhandled FormatException that the surrounding catch (SocketException/TimeoutException only) does not cover. This does not happen on the root -> .org -> iana.org path the article actually runs — I confirmed both referrals carry usable glue — but it is a real gap for a reader who edits `name` to a domain whose delegation lacks in-bailiwick glue.
issues.fixLooksLike: Check for an empty glueIp before the next Ask call and either resolve one of the delegated NS names via Dns.GetHostAddressesAsync as a fallback, or fail with a clear message; a sentence noting the program assumes every hop provides glue would also do, if the fallback is out of scope.
